newsitem.title: USA: FBI offers reward for Olympic bomber.
newsitem.headline: FBI offers reward for Olympic bomber.

text.p: The Federal Bureau of Investigation on Monday made public a telephone warning of the Olympic bombing and offered a reward for information leading to the arrest of the bomber or bombers.

The FBI announced it would pay "up to $500,000" for photographs, videotapes or information that helped them catch the person who planted the bomb on July 27 at Centennial Olympic Park during the 1996 Olympic Games.

Announcing the reward at a news conference in Atlanta, FBI deputy director Weldon Kennedy called the bombing, which killed two people and injured more than 100, a "vicious crime" and appealed to the public for help.
"We firmly believe that somewhere, someone has a photograph of this person carrying this bomb into the park," Kennedy said. "They may not know it. They may not realise they have it."
Agents played a tape of a terse telephone warning called in a short time before the bomb went off, telling authorities they had just a half-hour to act.
"There is a bomb in Centennial Park. You have 30 minutes," the male caller said.

The FBI has said very little about the bombing in the 4-1/2 months since the explosion. Security guard Richard Jewell, who alerted authorities to a knapsack containing the bomb, was initially identified as a suspect but was cleared on Oct. 26.
Kennedy said the bomb weighed about 40 lb (18 kg) and was carried in a green, military-style backpack. A similar pack was shown at the news conference.

He said a group of concert-goers reportedly "nudged" the backpack as it sat near the television light and sound tower where it eventually exploded. That nudge may have toppled the pack from an upright position to a horizontal one, saving lives by causing the main force of the blast to move vertically rather than horizontally.
"Indeed that turned out to be very fortunate, if in fact it was moved from the vertical position to the horizontal position, because no doubt that movement saved a lot of lives," Kennedy said.
The FBI denied the investigation had stalled and said its agents had interviewed hundreds of possible witnesses and reviewed thousands of photographs and videotapes.
"This investigation continues to have our highest priority," Kennedy said.

The agency asked for any photographs or videotapes taken in Olympic Park on Friday July 26 or Saturday July 27, and set up a toll-free hotline, 1-888-324-9797, for anyone with information about the bombing.
Kennedy said FBI experts had been unable to piece together a behavioural profile of the bomber because the motive for the bombing and the intended victims were unknown.
